_comment: Shipped defaults for the YourPHR TypeScript stack (yourphr#621). READ-ONLY: this file is the product, not the instance. An operator overrides values in <data dir>/config/app-custom-config.json, which holds ONLY what they changed — never a copy of this file. Keys prefixed with _ are comments and are ignored on load.
_comment_storage: yourphr#630 — YOURPHR_FAST_STORAGE and YOURPHR_SLOW_STORAGE are plain environment variables, not configuration keys: they are what LOCATE this file, so they cannot be set inside it. Both default to ./data, so a single-volume instance sets nothing. Fast holds small, hot, lock-dependent stores (the databases, config, .env); slow holds bulk and archives and is fine on a NAS. Every path below composes from one of them, so what goes where is decided HERE and not in code. SQLite must stay on the fast root — its locking is unsafe over NFS/SMB (yourphr#628).
_comment_environment_name: What this instance calls itself in the UI's version string — Go's web.environment_name. Published on /api/version as environment_name, and the ONLY source the footer has: the Angular bundle carries no name of its own, because one image serves every instance, so a name compiled in can only be a guess — and on yourphr#673 that guess told a production instance it was a sandbox. Set it either way: YOURPHR_WEB_ENVIRONMENT_NAME in <FAST_STORAGE>/.env, which is how a bare-metal operator running several daemons tells which one answered, or Admin -> Configuration when no variable is set. Deliberately NOT in config.env-keys: declared ownership would make the variable the only source and the screen read-only forever, and this key wants both doors. 'demo' on demo.yourphr.org, which is how a visitor tells the two apart; 'yourPHR' is what an instance that has not renamed itself shows.
_comment_auth_rate_limit: yourphr#647 — a per-IP FIXED WINDOW on the unauthenticated sign-in routes (/api/auth/signin and /api/auth/demo-signin). Separate from the throttle above, which counts FAILURES per account and per IP: this one counts REQUESTS, because demo sign-in runs a bcrypt verify for an anonymous caller who posts nothing, and a caller who never fails is not slowed by a failure counter. Setting max-requests to 0 or less turns it OFF, deliberately — an automated suite driving real logins from one address is the case that needs that switch. A non-positive window is a typo rather than an instruction, so it falls back to 60 seconds instead of reading as 'disable the backstop'. Counters are per PROCESS, so N replicas allow N times the budget.
_comment_demo: yourphr#643 — a PUBLIC DEMO signs every visitor into one shared account with POST /api/auth/demo-signin, which posts no credentials. `enabled` is published to callers with no login (the sign-in page decides whether to offer the button); the USERNAME is never published, and the password is verified server-side and never reaches a browser. The password is GENERATED at startup and written here as an override — nobody chooses it and nobody types it — and is regenerated whenever the stored hash and this value drift apart, which is what a freshly restored seed looks like. Leaving `enabled` false, the shipped default, makes every part of this inert.
_comment_demo_reset: yourphr#645 — the ONE setting in this product that deliberately destroys a live database. It is armed three ways: demo.enabled, demo.reset-on-restart, and a baseline.dir that actually holds one (no baseline, nothing to restore, nothing destroyed). Then it still has to PROVE the database belongs to a demo: every account in it must be the demo account, the demo admin, or the bootstrap admin, or the reset is refused and the instance starts normally WITH ITS DATA INTACT. An encrypted database is refused outright — the baseline ships in a public image, so it is plaintext. Sessions need no special handling: the session key is generated at every boot, so a restart already ends every session and a returning visitor gets the sign-in page.
_comment_demo_admin: yourphr#644 — the SECOND one-click entrance: a read-only admin tour, so a reviewer can see Configuration, Database and Logs without an operator handing out a real admin credential. Requires demo.admin.enabled ON TOP of demo.enabled, because an admin account a stranger can enter is not something one flag should be able to open. Same credential story as the demo account: the password is generated at startup, kept here, and verified server-side — the entrance posts nothing. The account holds the demo-admin ROLE, and every write is refused for it at the door regardless of what the UI renders.
_comment_chat: yourphr#594 - CHAT: ask a question about your own records in plain language. OFF by default and deliberately so: it needs a language-model endpoint an operator runs, and a feature that sends medical records to an LLM must be switched on by a person who decided to, never by a default. 'local' is the native provider - it searches your records where they already live, assembles the prompt here and calls your model directly, with no extra service. 'typesense' is the ported design, which keeps a second copy of every record in a sidecar; it survives for anyone already running it. 'null' is inert. Either way the model endpoint is yours and the caller's owner filter is applied server-side.
_comment_chat_model: Your model endpoint and the model on it. url is any OpenAI-compatible chat-completions host - for Ollama the bare address, no /v1 suffix. name is the model as that endpoint names it, with NO prefix: the 'vllm/' that the typesense provider requires is that engine's own convention and is added internally, not something an operator should have to know. model.id applies to the typesense provider only, where it is the CREATE-ONCE key: that engine freezes the prompt, endpoint and max-bytes into a conversation model on first use and ignores later edits, so changing any model value there means bumping the id too. The local provider has no such trap - its prompt takes effect on the next question.
yourphr.chat.model.name: llama3.1:8b
_comment_chat_max_bytes: Bytes of retrieved record text one answer may carry. 28672 was the Go default; 57344 was measured to give noticeably better answers where there is memory headroom on the model host, so that is the shipped value here.
_comment_chat_retrieval: How many of your records one answer may draw on. Measured against a 4B model on a real record: 5 records gave a clean correct answer, 10 correct with one stray item, 20 made it refuse outright, and 30 made it list blood tests as diagnoses. More context is NOT better - a smaller model degrades as it grows. Raise this only if you run a larger model and have checked that answers actually improve.
_comment_authorization: yourphr#623 — permissions and roles are DATA, read from the merged configuration at startup. The permission NAMES are the enforcement contract: a role may only name one this build defines, and an unknown name refuses the boot. roles.definitions is an object, so it deep-merges PER ROLE — an operator adds a role in app-custom-config.json without restating the others. A role's permissions[] is a plain list and is replaced wholesale on override, which is intended: it is one role's list, not the catalogue. issystem marks a role this build defines; it is not the operator's to redefine out of existence, because accounts store the role name.

admin-read.description: See the operator screens — configuration, database, logs, metrics, the provider catalog

admin-system.description: Change what this instance is — configuration values, instance identity, backups, the provider catalog

user-read.description: See the list of accounts and how many the instance holds

admin.description: Runs this instance: every operator screen, and the account list.

demo-admin.description: The public demo's admin tour (yourphr#644): every operator SCREEN and none of the writing. admin-read alone, deliberately — user-read is withheld because a stranger has no business reading the account list of an instance whose front door has no lock, and admin-system is what read-only means. Read-only is NOT enforced by this list alone: the routes answer curl whatever the UI renders, so the server refuses every write for this role by default (see the demo-admin guard).

user.description: Owns their own records. The empty list is not an oversight: a member reaches their own records by OWNERSHIP, not by a permission.

anonymous.description: A role with an empty list rather than an `if` at the edge, so the unauthenticated path goes through the same evaluator as every other.

_comment_public: Keys served by GET /api/instance/public to callers with NO login (yourphr#457). Direction matters: this is an ALLOW-LIST, so a key added anywhere else in this file is private until it is named here. A deny-list would publish anything nobody remembered to list. An instance may widen it in <data>/config/app-custom-config.json.
_comment_config_secret_keys: Keys masked on the Admin Configuration screen until an admin explicitly reveals one (yourphr#458). Deliberately SHORT: masking everything outside `public` makes an operator click through the listen port and the log level, and trains them to reveal reflexively. This list is the OPPOSITE shape to `public` and that is intentional — `public` is an allow-list because a mistake exposes a value to the internet; `secret` is a DENY-LIST because a mistake shows a value to an already-authenticated admin on their own screen. A value that is an ${VAR} environment reference masks itself and needs no entry here (yourphr#622).
_comment_config_env_keys: yourphr#635 — keys OWNED BY THE ENVIRONMENT, and the variable that supplies each. A key is owned by exactly one layer, never both: these are the environment's, so they are always read-only on Admin -> Configuration (409 on write) whether or not the variable is currently set, shown with the variable's name. Making ownership conditional on the variable being set would hand the screen the source of truth whenever it is absent, which is the ambiguity this removes. The value shipped below for such a key is a BOOT FALLBACK so a fresh install comes up, not a setting. To change one: set the variable in .env and restart. Nothing here writes .env, by design.
